body_markdown:
New World screwworm has been confirmed in a dog in Arizona, raising concerns about animal health, livestock safety, and the spread of this parasitic pest in the United States.


## Introduction


A confirmed case of New World screwworm in a dog in Arizona has raised fresh concerns about the spread of this dangerous parasitic pest in the United States. According to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), the infestation was identified in Cochise County, an area bordering Mexico.


The discovery marks another development in the ongoing effort to prevent the spread of New World screwworm, a parasitic fly whose larvae feed on the living tissue of warm-blooded animals. The incident also highlights the challenges facing animal health officials as they work to protect domestic animals, wildlife, and livestock.


Authorities have confirmed that the affected dog was receiving veterinary treatment. Officials are also implementing measures to monitor animals in the surrounding area and limit the risk of further transmission.


## What Is New World Screwworm?


New World screwworm is a parasitic fly scientifically known as *Cochliomyia hominivorax* . Unlike many other fly species whose larvae feed primarily on decaying organic material, screwworm larvae can develop in the living tissue of warm-blooded animals.


Female screwworm flies typically lay their eggs in open wounds or other suitable areas on an animal's body. Once the eggs hatch, the larvae enter the wound and feed on living tissue, potentially causing serious injury.


Without prompt treatment, an infestation can worsen and may become life-threatening.


The parasite can affect several types of animals, including cattle, horses, dogs, and wildlife. People can also become infested, although the risk to humans differs according to exposure and circumstances.


The ability of screwworm larvae to damage living tissue makes early detection and veterinary intervention particularly important.


## Screwworm Confirmed in an Arizona Dog


According to the Arizona Department of Agriculture, the recently identified case involved a dog in Cochise County. The animal had a wound on its back containing maggots consistent with a screwworm infestation.


Scientific testing subsequently confirmed the presence of the parasite.


The dog was receiving veterinary care following the discovery. State officials also indicated that preparations had been underway for the possibility of a local case.


Arizona State Veterinarian Dr. Ryan Wolker said authorities were responding quickly, reflecting concerns about the potential consequences of further spread.


The detection is significant because it extends the reported presence of screwworm in the United States beyond the previously affected areas of Texas and New Mexico.


However, a confirmed case does not automatically mean that the parasite has become established throughout Arizona. Continued surveillance and additional testing are necessary to determine whether other animals have been affected.


## USDA Introduces Measures to Contain the Infestation


Following the Arizona detection, federal authorities announced several measures intended to reduce the risk of further spread.


The USDA said it was restricting animal movement within approximately 20 kilometers, or 12 miles, of the affected location. The agency also planned to increase surveillance of live animals in the area.


Another important part of the response involves releasing sterile screwworm flies.


This approach is designed to reduce the parasite population. Sterile male flies mate with wild females but do not produce viable offspring, helping to interrupt the reproductive cycle over time.


When implemented consistently alongside surveillance and other control measures, the sterile insect technique can play an important role in managing screwworm populations.


Animal movement restrictions and inspections can also help officials identify additional cases before the infestation spreads further.


The effectiveness of these measures will depend on continued monitoring, timely reporting, and cooperation among federal agencies, state authorities, veterinarians, and animal owners.


## Screwworm Cases Increase Across the United States


The Arizona case comes amid broader concerns about the return of New World screwworm to the United States.


The parasite was eradicated from the country decades ago through extensive control efforts. However, its northward spread through parts of Latin America and Mexico has increased pressure on US animal health authorities.


According to information published by the USDA and reported by Reuters, officials had recorded 71 screwworm cases since June as of October 28, 2026. Eighteen of those cases were reported as active at that time.


The reported number of active infestations had increased substantially compared with the previous month, when only two active cases were recorded.


Earlier detections included cases involving cattle in Texas and New Mexico. Authorities also recently confirmed an infestation in an elk in Texas, marking a reported case in US wildlife.


These developments underline the importance of monitoring both domesticated animals and wildlife.


Because animals can move across regions and national borders, early identification and coordinated disease-control measures remain essential to preventing additional outbreaks.


## Impact on Livestock and Beef Prices


The screwworm situation is also affecting agricultural trade and raising concerns about livestock production.


In an effort to prevent the parasite from entering the United States, the USDA suspended livestock imports from Mexico in 2025. The restrictions affected cross-border cattle trade and contributed to concerns about an already tight domestic cattle supply.


Limited cattle availability has been one factor associated with elevated beef prices in the United States. However, beef prices are influenced by several other factors, including herd sizes, production costs, consumer demand, and broader market conditions.


The USDA began gradually resuming certain livestock imports from Mexico in August 2026, reopening trade at three ports of entry in Arizona and New Mexico.


Officials had also indicated that livestock imports through Nogales, Arizona, could resume on November 30, 2026, provided the necessary safety conditions were met.


The latest Arizona screwworm detection could complicate those plans if authorities determine that additional restrictions are necessary.


Any decisions about reopening trade will depend on disease surveillance, veterinary safeguards, and assessments of the risk to US livestock.


## Signs of Screwworm Infestation in Dogs


Pet owners should pay attention to wounds that appear unusual or deteriorate unexpectedly.


Potential warning signs of a screwworm infestation include:


- Open wounds containing visible larvae or maggots.
- Wounds that become larger or increasingly damaged.
- Unusual discharge or a strong odor coming from an injured area.
- Persistent licking, scratching, or biting around a wound.
- Signs of pain, restlessness, or changes in behavior.
- Reduced appetite or weakness in more serious cases.


These symptoms are not exclusive to screwworm and can occur with other infections or injuries. A veterinary examination is necessary to determine the cause.


Pet owners should seek prompt veterinary attention if they discover larvae in a wound or notice rapidly worsening tissue damage.


Avoid attempting to treat a suspected screwworm infestation at home. A veterinarian can examine the wound, remove larvae safely, assess tissue damage, and determine the appropriate treatment.


People who live in affected areas should also follow official animal health guidance and report suspicious infestations to the appropriate state agricultural authorities.


## What Happens Next?


The coming weeks will be important for determining whether the Arizona detection represents an isolated incident or part of a wider pattern of transmission.


Authorities are expected to rely on surveillance, laboratory testing, movement controls, and other established pest-management measures to identify potential additional cases.


Animal owners, ranchers, wildlife professionals, and veterinarians can support these efforts by checking animals for unusual wounds and reporting suspected infestations promptly.


Residents should rely on official updates from the USDA and the Arizona Department of Agriculture for information about local restrictions and recommended precautions.


Although the detection is concerning, the response measures are intended to contain the risk and prevent the parasite from becoming established in new areas.


## Conclusion


The confirmation of New World screwworm in an Arizona dog represents another challenge for US animal health officials. With cases previously reported in Texas and New Mexico, the discovery highlights the importance of continued surveillance and rapid intervention.


The parasite can cause severe tissue damage in animals, making early detection and veterinary care essential. At the same time, restrictions on animal movement and the use of sterile flies demonstrate how authorities are working to control the threat.


For pet owners and livestock producers, awareness and prompt reporting remain important steps in protecting animal health.


As the situation develops, updates from official agricultural authorities will help clarify the extent of the risk and guide further control efforts.
